title: Why You Can't Swat a Fly: Animals That See in Slow Motion
description: Animal Secrets #21. To a fly, your hand moves in slow motion. We count down five animals that live in fast-forward: your dog, the swordfish that heats its own eyes, the pied flycatcher, the blow fly and dragonfly at 300 flashes per second, and #1, the crow, whose brain just beat humans and monkeys in a speed test published in Science this month. Part of the Wild Sketchbook.

scenes.say: Try to swat a fly, and it's gone before your hand lands. Ever wonder why?

scenes.label: Your hand = slow-mo
scenes.say: Here's the thing. To that fly, your hand isn't fast. It's floating toward it, almost in slow motion.

scenes.label: Saved for #1
scenes.say: And today we count down five animals that live in fast-forward. Stay for number one, because it doesn't just see faster than you.
It thinks faster than you. A brand new study in the journal Science just timed it, and the number is wild.

scenes.label: How fast is 'fast'?
scenes.say: Okay, so first, how do you even measure how fast an animal sees? You can't exactly ask a fly.
Scientists use a flickering light. They speed it up until the flashing blurs into one steady glow.

scenes.label: Humans: 65 Hz
scenes.say: That blur point is called the critical flicker fusion frequency. For you, it's around 65 flashes per second.
Above that, your brain just gives up and sees a smooth light. That's basically your frame rate.
Movies and TV trick you with this all the time. They flash still pictures fast enough that your brain stitches them into motion.

scenes.label: 100+ animals compared
scenes.say: Now here's where it gets weird. In 2022, researcher Kevin Healy compared this number across more than a hundred animals.

scenes.label: 0.7 Hz
scenes.say: The slowest one? The crown-of-thorns starfish, at just 0.7 flashes per second. Less than one!
For that starfish, a whole second of your life is less than one blurry snapshot.

scenes.label: 4 per second
scenes.say: And an earlier study found deep-sea isopods, relatives of the woodlouse, could only see a light flick on and off four times a second.
The pattern? Big, slow animals, like large turtles, tend to take in less information per second.
Not because they're dumb. A big body with a slow engine just doesn't need to react in a split second.
Small, fast animals with a racing metabolism take in more. Their world plays like a slowed-down movie.
Researchers think time itself may feel different to them. More moments packed into every single second.

scenes.label: Fly, small, or sea
scenes.say: And the fastest of all tend to share three traits. They fly, they're small, or they hunt in the sea. Keep that in mind.

scenes.label: #5 Your dog
scenes.say: So let's start the countdown with the one sitting on your couch right now. Your dog.

scenes.label: Dogs: 75 Hz
scenes.say: Dogs come in at around 75 flashes per second. That's faster than your 65.
And that explains something weird. Older TV screens flickered at a rate that looked smooth to you.
But researchers say dogs could see the flicker, because their eyes refresh faster than the screen did.
Think about that. You were watching a movie. Your dog was watching a strobe light.
So if your dog ever seemed bored by the TV, maybe it wasn't the show. Maybe it was the flicker.
Now, a dog is only a little faster than us. The next animal had to cheat to win.

scenes.label: #4 Swordfish
scenes.say: Number four. The swordfish. And it hunts in a place that should make its eyes slow.

scenes.label: Water: 3 °C
scenes.say: Swordfish dive several hundred metres down, into water as cold as three degrees Celsius.
Here's the problem. Cold eyes are slow eyes. A cold fish sees the world like a laggy video call.
And down there, its prey, like fast squid, is zipping around in the dark.

scenes.label: Salmon: 96 Hz
scenes.say: For comparison, a salmon scores around 96 flashes per second. Good, but not good enough for a deep, cold chase.

scenes.label: Built-in heater
scenes.say: So the swordfish does something almost no animal does. It turns on a heater. Right behind its eyes.

scenes.label: +10 to 15 °C
scenes.say: A special eye muscle burns energy just to make heat. It warms the eyes and brain up to 10 to 15 degrees above the water.

scenes.label: 10x sharper timing
scenes.say: And the payoff is huge. A 2005 study found its vision can track changes more than ten times better than fish with cold eyes.
So while the squid sees a blur, the swordfish sees every twist and turn. Basically, night vision with heated seats.
Remember that list? Small, flying, or hunting in the sea. The swordfish wins its spot with pure sea-hunter engineering.
But here's the twist. To beat 65, you don't need a heater. You just need to be small and fast.

scenes.label: #3 Pied flycatcher
scenes.say: Number three. This little bird is the pied flycatcher, a tiny songbird that hunts on the wing.

scenes.label: 146 Hz
scenes.say: Its flicker number is 146 flashes per second. That's more than double yours.

scenes.label: Fastest vertebrate
scenes.say: According to Healy's comparison, that's the fastest eyes of any animal with a backbone.
And it makes total sense once you know its job. It catches flying insects, in the air, while dodging branches.
Miss by a fraction of a second, and lunch is gone. So evolution turned its eyes into a high-speed camera.
If you watched a flycatcher hunt, you'd see a blur. In its head, the insect is drifting by like a balloon.
That's the small and flying combo from earlier, and it pays off big. But it still isn't the overall winner.
Okay, quick check. If 146 is the fastest backbone animal, who on Earth beats it?
The answer is tiny, it's buzzing, and you've probably tried to kill one this week.

scenes.label: #2 Blow flies
scenes.say: Number two. Blow flies. Those shiny green and blue ones that find your picnic in seconds.

scenes.label: 300 Hz
scenes.say: Their eyes handle around 300 flashes per second. That's more than four times faster than you.

scenes.label: Dragonflies: 300 Hz
scenes.say: Dragonflies hit the same 300. And they're some of the best hunters in the whole insect world.
Now picture being a mosquito, trying to escape a hunter that sees your every wingbeat in slow motion.

scenes.label: Study: 30+ species
scenes.say: A 2013 study from Trinity College Dublin compared more than 30 species and saw the same thing.
The lead researcher put it simply. Flies can see light flickering up to four times faster than we can.

scenes.label: Matrix-style
scenes.say: So when you swing, the fly basically watches it like the bullet-dodging scene in a movie.

scenes.label: Too fast to see
scenes.say: But speed has a limit. One tiger beetle runs so fast, its eyes can't keep up. It has to stop to look.
Imagine sprinting so fast that the world turns into a blur, so you keep stopping just to check where you are.
So even nature's fastest eyes have a speed cap. And that brings us to the strangest one.

scenes.label: #1 The crow
scenes.say: Number one. The crow. And no, its eyes aren't the record breakers here. Its brain is.

scenes.label: Tübingen, 2026
scenes.say: In 2026, scientists at the University of Tübingen in Germany ran a speed test on two carrion crows.
The task looked simple. Dots moved on a touchscreen, and the crow had to peck left or right.
Which way are the dots moving? Decide. Go. Humans and monkeys have done this exact kind of test for years.

scenes.label: 235 ms
scenes.say: The crows answered in an average of 235 milliseconds. That's about a quarter of a second.

scenes.label: 2x faster than you
scenes.say: And that's about twice as fast as humans and monkeys. Twice.

scenes.label: Nearly 100% right
scenes.say: With clear signals, they were nearly 100 percent right. So they weren't guessing. They were just fast.
Then the scientists listened to the crows' brain cells while they decided.

scenes.label: 70 ms
scenes.say: About 70 milliseconds after the dots appeared, the neurons were already splitting into 'left' and 'right'.
The crow was making up its mind before you'd even notice the dots had moved.
Here's the crazy part. The brain signals looked a lot like the ones seen in humans and monkeys. Same plan, much faster.
That matters, because bird brains are built very differently from ours. Different wiring, yet the same kind of decision, done quicker.
So why? Honestly, nobody knows yet. The researchers think flying and using a beak may demand split-second choices.
Crows, ravens and magpies are already famous for being smart. Now we know they're quick too.
So the bird watching you from the fence isn't just remembering things. It may be deciding things faster than you can.
So next time a fly dodges you, remember. To it, you're the slow one.
Fun fact. Some research suggests goalkeepers and even coffee can briefly speed up how fast humans perceive things.
But you'd still lose a decision race to a crow. So, which animal surprised you most? Tell me in the comments.

short.title: Crows Just Beat Humans at a Speed Test
short.description: Two carrion crows, one touchscreen, 235 milliseconds. A new Science study (University of Tübingen, 2026) found crows decide about twice as fast as humans and monkeys. Full countdown on my channel.

scenes.say: Crows decide twice as fast as you. Scientists just timed it.
Two carrion crows watched dots move on a touchscreen. Left or right? Peck.
Their average answer took 235 milliseconds. That's about a quarter of a second.
And they were nearly 100 percent right. Humans and monkeys? About half as fast.
The craziest part is inside the brain. Just 70 milliseconds after the dots appeared, its neurons were already choosing a side.
Same kind of brain signals as humans and monkeys. Just way faster. The study came out this year in Science.
So next time a crow stares at you from a fence, remember this. Crows decide twice as fast as you.
